title: Bidirectional BFS in NYC: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch two BFS waves launch from start and goal and meet in the middle to shrink the search space. This city-grid visualization shows why Bidirectional BFS is a graph optimization that can feel instant compared to plain BFS.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — two simultaneous searches can halve the work ⚡

Imagine routing across Midtown’s grid. Instead of exploring outward from just your start, we run BFS from BOTH ends:
• Forward frontier expands from the start
• Backward frontier expands from the goal
• The moment the frontiers touch, we’ve found the shortest path

Why it’s faster: if each BFS step branches ~b and the shortest path length is d, then:
• Normal BFS explores ~b^d
• Bidirectional BFS explores ~2·b^(d/2)
That exponent change is the whole superpower (meeting in the middle).

Coding interview prep takeaway: when edges are unweighted and you need the shortest path, consider Bidirectional BFS as a graph optimization—especially when the graph is large.

Debate question: In which scenario would you *not* use Bidirectional BFS—small graphs, directed graphs, or when memory is tight?
